title: Consistency Regularisation for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation in Monocular Depth Estimation
abstract: Monocular depth estimation models trained on one domain (e.g. synthetic or a specific camera setup) typically degrade sharply when applied to a new, unlabelled target domain, and existing unsupervised domain adaptation solutions usually require training multiple separate models or following complex multi-stage protocols. This work reframes the adaptation problem as a consistency-based semi-supervised learning task: the model is trained with full supervision only on the labelled source domain, while on the unlabelled target domain it is encouraged to produce depth predictions that stay consistent across different augmented views or perturbations of the same input. This removes the need for target-domain ground truth or auxiliary adaptation networks entirely. The approach is evaluated on the standard KITTI and NYUv2 monocular depth benchmarks under several source-to-target domain shifts, where it matches or exceeds prior unsupervised domain adaptation methods for depth estimation while using a substantially simpler, single-model training pipeline.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Likelihood Ratio Estimation for Pixel-Wise Out-of-Distribution Detection
abstract: Semantic segmentation models used in autonomous driving are trained on a fixed set of known classes and tend to confidently mislabel unknown objects as one of those classes, which is dangerous in open-world deployment. Pixel-wise out-of-distribution (OoD) detection addresses this by flagging unknown-object pixels, but existing outlier-exposure methods struggle to tell apart truly unknown objects from merely rare in-distribution classes, since both trigger high uncertainty in the base segmentation model. This paper introduces an uncertainty-aware likelihood-ratio test built on an evidential classifier, which outputs full probability distributions rather than point estimates, explicitly separating uncertainty caused by rare training examples from uncertainty caused by imperfect synthetic OoD proxies used during training. This lets outlier exposure be used more effectively without conflating the two sources of uncertainty. Evaluated on five standard urban-driving OoD benchmarks, the method achieves the lowest average false-positive rate among compared state-of-the-art approaches while keeping high average precision, at negligible extra computational cost over the base segmentation model.

title: GroupEnsemble: Efficient Uncertainty Estimation for DETR-based Object Detection
abstract: Reliable object detectors need to quantify both semantic uncertainty (is this really an object, and of which class?) and spatial uncertainty (exactly where and how large is it?), which is safety-critical for autonomous driving. Standard ensemble-based uncertainty estimation (e.g. Deep Ensembles) is accurate but expensive, requiring several independently trained models. This paper proposes GroupEnsemble, which exploits the query-based structure of DETR-style detectors: instead of training multiple full models, several diverse groups of object queries are passed through one shared decoder in a single forward pass, with an attention mask preventing the groups from interacting, so each group produces an independent detection set that can be treated as one ensemble member. This yields ensemble-style uncertainty estimates without the memory and training cost of independently trained models. Tested on Cityscapes (autonomous-driving scenes) and COCO (everyday scenes), a hybrid of GroupEnsemble with MC-Dropout outperforms full Deep Ensembles on several calibration and detection-quality metrics at a fraction of the computational cost.

title: Detecting and Mitigating Memorization in Diffusion Models through Anisotropy of the Log-Probability
abstract: Diffusion models can memorize and later reproduce near-exact copies of specific training images, which raises data-privacy and copyright concerns and can bias evaluation benchmarks. Existing lightweight memorization detectors rely on the norm of the difference between conditional and unconditional denoising scores, which this paper shows is only a reliable signal when the underlying log-probability landscape is roughly isotropic -- true at medium-to-high noise levels, but not at the low-noise levels most relevant to fine image detail. Analysing the low-noise, anisotropic regime instead, the authors find that memorized samples show unusually strong angular alignment between the guidance vector and the unconditional score. Combining this angular-alignment signal with the existing norm-based signal yields a new detection metric that can be computed directly from pure-noise inputs via just two forward passes, avoiding any costly iterative denoising. On Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2, the combined metric outperforms prior denoising-free detectors while running roughly five times faster than the previous best approach, and the paper further shows the metric can guide a practical mitigation strategy that adapts memorized prompts.

title: Forecasting the Past: Gradient-Based Distribution Shift Detection in Trajectory Prediction
abstract: Trajectory-prediction models for automated driving are trained on a limited range of driving situations and can silently fail -- producing confident but wrong forecasts -- when deployed on out-of-distribution situations such as unusual manoeuvres, unfamiliar layouts, or rare weather. This paper proposes a lightweight, post-hoc distribution-shift detector that does not touch or retrain the original prediction model at all. A small decoder is trained, after the fact, on a self-supervised auxiliary task: forecasting the second half of an already-observed trajectory from its first half. The L2 norm of the gradient of this auxiliary forecasting loss, computed with respect to the decoder's final layer, is then used directly as a distribution-shift score for new inputs -- a large gradient indicates a trajectory unlike anything the decoder learned to forecast well. The method is validated on the Shifts and Argoverse trajectory-prediction benchmarks, where it substantially improves distribution-shift detection over baselines, and is further shown able to give early warning of simulated collisions for a reinforcement-learning motion planner in a highway driving simulator.

title: Diffusion Model Guided Sampling with Pixel-Wise Aleatoric Uncertainty Estimation
abstract: Diffusion models can generate high-quality images, but during sampling there is no built-in, computationally cheap signal for which pixels or regions the model is still uncertain about -- existing uncertainty-estimation techniques such as MC-Dropout or deep ensembles require special training or multiple full models, and are impractical to apply at scale to diffusion sampling. This paper proposes a training-free method that estimates pixel-wise aleatoric uncertainty directly during the normal sampling process, by measuring the sensitivity of the denoising output to small perturbations of the same input at a given noise level. The authors show this sensitivity-based uncertainty measure is theoretically connected to the second derivative of the noise distribution, giving it a principled interpretation: pixels with high estimated uncertainty correspond to fine details the model finds hardest to reconstruct consistently. Rather than only reporting this uncertainty, the method actively steers the sampling process toward the high-uncertainty regions identified, which is shown to improve final image quality, measured by FID, over standard sampling on both ImageNet and CIFAR-10.
